 jph@gwu.edu

The bottleneck on what you can build is no longer what you already know — it’s your workflow discipline and your ability to direct an agent. This course teaches students to use tools like Claude Code to build ambitious things they don’t yet know how to build, while developing the professional engineering workflows — version control with Git and GitHub, continuous integration with GitHub Actions, and deployment with GitHub Pages — that make agentic work sustainable and trustworthy. Each week pairs a hands-on workflow concept (taught live in class) with an ambitious take-home build in an unfamiliar domain: a deployed personal website, a novel in an author’s voice, a video game, a data pipeline, a simulation experiment, and more. The arc of the course follows a “trust gradient,” moving from high-touch, back-and-forth collaboration with an agent toward orchestrating specialized agents that work for long stretches under human supervision. By the end, students will have strong, transferable engineering workflow skills, the ability to work with code and data through an agent, and — most importantly — the ability to teach themselves new domains so they can tackle harder systems in the future.



Students must have completed at least one programming course (e.g., CSCI 1012 or equivalent) or have comparable experience working in at least one programming language. You do not need to be an expert, but you should be comfortable reading code, following the logic of a program, and recognizing when something is wrong — these are the skills that let you supervise an agent rather than blindly trust it. Students with zero coding experience will find this course very difficult.

title: Syllabus
text:
Participation & Attendance
Attendance will be taken and is the primary driver of your participation grade.
In-class work is hands-on and ungraded — but it is practice for the build you do at home. The take-home builds assume the skills we develop together in class, so missing class costs you twice: once on participation, and again on a much harder homework. Plan to attend in person every week.

title: Syllabus
text:
Individual Builds
Each week (Weeks 1–8) you complete one build: an ambitious project in a domain you likely haven’t worked in before. Each build is delivered as a GitHub repository that includes the full conversation history with the agent. Grading focuses on prompt quality, evidence of iterative collaboration, final product quality, and thoughtful use of the week’s workflow skill. There are 8 builds, each worth 5% of your grade.

title: Syllabus
text:
Team Project
Throughout the semester you’ll work in teams of 3–4 on an open-ended project of your own design — the one piece of fully open-ended work in the course. It is broken into milestone deliverables (proposal, interim report, final report, presentation). See the project overview for details.

title: Syllabus
text:
Generative-AI Use Policy
Using AI agents is not “cheating” in this course — it is the core skill being taught. For individual builds you are required to use an agentic coding tool and to disclose your full conversation history as part of your submission. You remain fully responsible for the correctness, quality, and originality of everything you submit: read what the agent produces, run it, and fix it when it’s wrong. Detailed disclosure requirements appear in each assignment.

title: Team Project Overview
text:
The team project is the capstone of the course — and the only piece of fully open-ended work. In teams of 3–4, you’ll propose and build an ambitious, real-world project of your own design, applying every workflow skill from the semester: version control, planning, skills, automation, debugging, continuous integration, deployment, and (where it helps) multi-agent orchestration.
Throughout the final weeks, class sessions become team work sessions where the instructor circulates, audits progress, and gives direction — and where we learn collaboration workflows (pull request reviews, issues, and fork → branch → merge) live, as you need them.

Description:
The bottleneck on what you can build is no longer what you already know — it’s your workflow discipline and your ability to direct an agent. This course teaches students to use tools like Claude Code to build ambitious things they don’t yet know how to build, while developing the professional engineering workflows — version control with Git and GitHub, continuous integration with GitHub Actions, and deployment with GitHub Pages — that make agentic work sustainable and trustworthy. Each week pairs a hands-on workflow concept (taught live in class) with an ambitious take-home build in an unfamiliar domain: a deployed personal website, a novel in an author’s voice, a video game, a data pipeline, a simulation experiment, and more. By the end, students will have strong, transferable engineering workflow skills, the ability to work with code and data through an agent, and — most importantly — the ability to teach themselves new domains so they can tackle harder systems in the future.
Learning Objectives:
Having successfully completed this course, students will be able to:

Direct an AI agent to build real products in domains they haven’t learned before.
Use Git, GitHub, and pull requests fluently as everyday version control and collaboration tools.
Set up continuous integration with GitHub Actions and deploy to the web with GitHub Pages.
Debug agent-built systems and use agents to diagnose and resolve issues, with automated review.
Orchestrate specialized agents (planning, coding, testing) into a supervised pipeline.
Teach themselves a new domain using an agent — the meta-skill that outlasts any single tool.

Prerequisites:
Students must have completed at least one programming course (e.g., CSCI 1012 or equivalent) or have comparable experience working in at least one programming language. You do not need to be an expert, but you should be comfortable reading code, following the logic of a program, and recognizing when something is wrong — these are the skills that let you supervise an agent rather than blindly trust it. Students with zero coding experience will find this course very difficult.
